title: Focusing on preeclampsia risk: The clinical value of blood-based biomarkers
summary: When do you start screening for preeclampsia? Learn how biomarkers for preeclampsia can improve risk assessment across pregnancy.
body_markdown:
Preeclampsia remains one of the most serious and unpredictable complications in pregnancy. Current professional medical society screening guidelines rely heavily on maternal history and clinical risk factors. While important, these methods do not detect all patients who will develop preeclampsia. That means some at-risk pregnancies may go unidentified until complications arise, limiting your ability to intervene proactively.


Evidence reinforces this limitation. In the[SPREE study](https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/uog.19039) , screening based on traditional guidelines detected approximately 30% of all preeclampsia cases and 41% of preterm preeclampsia cases.


This creates a familiar clinical dilemma. Patients without classic risk factors may still develop preeclampsia, while those identified as high risk may not go on to develop the condition. This uncertainty can complicate decisions around monitoring, referrals, and preventive therapy.


**The solution: Biomarkers add clarity to preeclampsia risk assessment**


Blood-based biomarkers provide objective, physiologic insight into placental function and disease progression. When used together with assessment of clinical factors, they significantly improve detection rates. By integrating biomarker testing into routine care, you can identify at-risk patients earlier, make more confident clinical decisions, and improve outcomes for both pregnant patients and babies.


Emerging evidence suggests that biomarker-informed screening can improve confidence at both ends of the risk spectrum. A recent[study](https://www.ajogmfm.org/article/S2589-9333(26)00067-4/abstract) of more than 7,300 pregnancies found that patients with low placental growth factor (PlGF) levels and a low-risk result from a combined first-trimester preeclampsia screening algorithm were not at increased risk for preeclampsia, stillbirth, or maternal or neonatal morbidity. These findings highlight the value of multimarker risk assessment, which can help identify patients who may benefit from closer surveillance while also providing reassurance when overall predicted risk remains low.


Research shows that integrating these biomarkers into screening models improves detection. In the SPREE study, combining maternal factors with biomarkers increased detection of preterm preeclampsia to as high as 82%.


Similarly, first-trimester multimarker approaches demonstrated detection rates of about 77% for preterm preeclampsia in the[ASPRE trial](https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/uog.18816) .


Together, this data suggests a more comprehensive and precise view of patient risk through a multibiomarker approach.


**Identifying patients at risk of preeclampsia who might otherwise be missed**


One of the most important advantages of biomarker testing is its ability to identify patients who appear low risk based on traditional criteria.


Incorporating biomarkers can help:


- Detect subtle placental abnormalities earlier
- Identify patients who may benefit from closer surveillance
- Avoid false reassurance in “low-risk” populations


**When to consider using a preeclampsia blood-based biomarker**


Preeclampsia risk evolves throughout pregnancy. Biomarker testing can provide clinically actionable information at multiple stages of care.


***First-trimester preeclampsia screening (11 to 14 weeks’ gestation)***


This screening can help identify patients early in pregnancy who may not initially be considered at high risk. Patients who are found to be at an increased risk can gain access to aspirin prophylaxis and informed surveillance and care planning.


**Key biomarkers for the first-trimester preeclampsia screen:**


- Placental growth factor (PlGF)
- Pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPP-A)


***Second- and third-trimester preeclampsia testing (23 to 34.9 weeks’ gestation)***


This test can help evaluate the risk for progression from mild preeclampsia to preeclampsia with severe features and support decisions regarding monitoring, referral, hospitalization, and delivery planning.


**Key biomarkers for the second- and third-trimester preeclampsia test:**


- Soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1)
- Placental growth factor (PlGF)


This is particularly relevant in time-sensitive clinical presentations, including new-onset hypertension in hospitalized patients, borderline or atypical symptoms, and cases of diagnostic uncertainty, where rapid biomarker results can provide the clarity needed to triage patients appropriately.


The[PRAECIS study](https://womenshealth.labcorp.com/sites/default/files/2024-03/Flyer_PNS_PRAECIS_US_BMKT001051.1_EN%20%281%29.pdf) demonstrated that the sFlt-1/PlGF ratio can effectively predict progression to severe preeclampsia within two weeks, with a high sensitivity and high negative predictive value. For hospitalized patients presenting with mild preeclampsia or hypertensive disorders, this information can help distinguish those who may require escalated management from those appropriate for expectant management.


This high negative predictive value also supports avoidance of unnecessary continued hospitalizations, helping to focus resources on patients who require immediate escalation of care, while reducing stress and limiting inconvenience for patients at lower risk.


**The right preeclampsia biomarker test at the right clinical moment**


Preeclampsia risk doesn't look the same at 12 weeks as it does at 28 weeks, and neither should your assessment approach. Labcorp offers two distinct, evidence-based blood tests designed for two different clinical questions at two different points in pregnancy across the continuum of care.
